questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] subscription invoicing and dunning for a multi-tenant billing platform (organized-study-enterprise-billing-platform, docs/system-design-current.md). Scenario: the platform bills on behalf of 8,000 tenant organizations holding 60,000 subscriptions between them. Renewal dates cluster, so about 70% of each month's invoices must be generated within one hour on the 1st; each invoice is the plan price per seat with a coupon and tax applied; about 3% of charges are declined, and the dunning policy is three charges over ten days and then suspension. Write your design before you look: what makes an invoice one document for one subscription and one period, how renewals are found and turned into invoices at that peak, how invoice numbers are assigned, how the lines and totals are computed and kept, which states an invoice and a subscription move through during dunning and which moves are legal, and how the work splits between the API and the worker. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] An invoice's identity is subscription plus period, stored and enforced: today the only duplicate guard is in the worker, which looks for an invoice whose creation time falls inside the subscription's current window, so the design stores period start and end on the invoice and adds a unique rule on subscription and period start, making a second generation for one period a refused insert rather than a lucky read.

[w3] Renewals are found by a scheduled sweep, which the repo plans but does not have: a repeatable job selects active subscriptions whose period has ended, advances the period, and enqueues one generation job per subscription with a job id built from subscription and period start, so the sweep can run again without producing anything new.

[w2] The peak is about 42,000 invoices in an hour, roughly 12 a second, which a modest worker pool absorbs if each job reads its period from the subscription row; due date and finalization time are stamped from the wall clock at generation today (due 14 days after 'now'), so a job that runs late quietly moves the due date, and the design anchors both to the period instead.

[w3] Numbers cannot come from counting: the number is the organization's invoice count plus one, under a unique rule per organization, so two invoices generated at once for a large tenant compute the same number and one transaction fails; a per-organization counter row incremented inside the generating transaction gives gap-free numbers that cannot collide, at the price of serialising that tenant's generation on one row, which is cheap at about 12 invoices a second across the fleet.

[w3] Totals are computed once, in integer cents, and frozen on the document: the worker writes each line and the subtotal, discount, tax and total onto the invoice row at generation, so a later price, coupon or tax-rate change never reprices an invoice that has already been issued.

[w2] Coupon and tax must belong to the subscription or customer: generation currently takes the organization's newest active coupon and any active tax rate, so every subscriber of a tenant gets the same discount and tax; the design references a redeemed coupon (with its validity window) on the subscription, a tax rate per customer jurisdiction, and records on the invoice which ones priced it.

[w3] Dunning runs on the transitions the domain already declares (an open invoice may become paid, void or uncollectible, and an uncollectible one may still become paid; an active subscription may fall to past due, which may return to active or end as canceled), although no workflow calls those helpers yet; the ladder is decline then past due, a second and third charge on a schedule, then the invoice marked uncollectible and access suspended. Past due cannot move to paused, so suspension is either a new state or an access flag on past due.

[w2] The API accepts and queues while the worker generates and charges, but generation exists twice, once in the worker and once behind a manual endpoint that skips the period guard, so the split starts by extracting one shared generation function that both paths call.
keyPoints.quote: The worker and API duplicate some invoice-generation shape; a future service extraction can reduce that.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the first month at full volume. The 1st's backlog drains slowly and some invoice jobs run after midnight, on the 2nd; one subscription's generation job runs twice for the same period; a tenant deactivates a coupon after its customer has seen an invoice preview but before the invoice is generated; and a subscriber suspended by dunning pays the open invoice on day 12. What breaks, how does each problem show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The period guard is only as good as the window it reads at run time: it compares the invoice's creation time, which is the wall clock, with the subscription's current window, so a job draining onto the 2nd still lands inside its window, but a job that runs after the period has ended and before the window advances writes an invoice no later check can ever match, so every rerun bills again, and no invoice records which period it billed. With period columns, the job carries the period it was created for and the unique rule settles it.

[w3] Two runs both pass a check-then-insert: each transaction reads 'no invoice yet' before either inserts, and nothing locks the subscription or rejects the second row; the manual endpoint has no period check at all, and neither path looks at the subscription's status, so a subscription that starts in its trial (the default) is billed in full as soon as it is created. The unique rule turns the second run into a conflict that the job treats as already done.

[w2] The coupon change reprices silently: there is no preview record and no coupon on the subscription, so generation picks whatever coupon is newest and active at that moment, perhaps a different one or none; the design either issues the preview from the same stored inputs the invoice will use or labels it an estimate, and records the coupon that priced the final document.

[w3] Paying during suspension must be a legal path back, not an accident: the declared moves allow uncollectible to paid and past due to active, so the payment path should apply both in one step; at this commit nothing in the code ever changes a subscription's status after it is created, so a subscriber who pays on day 12 would stay suspended until someone intervenes by hand.

[w2] Reactivation is one transaction (payment recorded, invoice paid, subscription active, access restored, audit and outbox rows written), and every later dunning step re-reads the invoice's state first, so the day-10 charge for an invoice already paid does nothing.

[w2] A failed job is a silent miss: jobs are added with no attempts, backoff or job id, so under the queue's defaults a generation that fails, for example on a number collision, is never retried and the subscription is never billed; a nightly reconciliation lists subscriptions with an ended period and no invoice for it.

[w1] Dunning reminders are a delivery problem of their own: give each reminder an id derived from the invoice and the attempt number and hand it to the mail provider as an idempotency key, so a reminder replayed after a worker crash is suppressed downstream instead of reaching the customer twice; the failed-payment event already carries the payment and invoice ids that key is built from.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your billing design against the alternatives: a renewal sweep that generates invoices versus a delayed job scheduled for each subscription's next renewal; a mid-cycle plan change handled as a proration credit versus an adjustment on the next invoice; a fixed dunning schedule versus smart retries timed to the decline reason; hard suspension versus degraded service; and calendar billing on the 1st versus each subscription's own anniversary. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A sweep is one re-runnable query (due subscriptions with no invoice for the period) that also repairs missed jobs, at the cost of the 1st-of-month spike and a scan; a delayed job per subscription spreads load by itself, but it lives only in Redis, and the repo already shows a committed subscription left with nothing queued when Redis was down, so the sweep stays as the safety net either way.
keyPoints.quote: the subscription exists, has no invoice job

keyPoints.text: [w3] Proration is a declared supposition here: a subscription holds one plan, one seat count and one current period, and nothing changes a plan mid-cycle. Supposing that path, a proration credit is exact and immediate but multiplies documents (a credit and a new charge per change), while adjusting the next invoice keeps one invoice per period at the cost of an upgrade billed late or a downgrade refunded late.

[w2] A fixed schedule is predictable, testable and easy to explain in reminder emails; reason-aware timing (retry after payday for insufficient funds, ask for a new card when it expired) recovers more revenue but is opaque and needs data; the payment row already keeps a failure code and message, the raw input for the second approach.

[w3] Hard suspension collects fastest but punishes the subscriber's own users and invites churn; degrading (read-only, no new seats) keeps goodwill and stretches the timeline; either needs a home in the state model, because paused is reachable only from active and past due leads only to active or canceled.

[w2] Periods today start when the subscription is created and last a number of days (30 by default), so they drift across calendar months; billing everyone on the 1st simplifies reporting and proration but creates the peak, while anniversary billing spreads 60,000 invoices to about 2,000 a day, which is the cheaper capacity plan.
[w1] Keeping invoice, payment and subscription changes inside one database is what makes each dunning move a single transaction; extracting billing into its own service later would trade that away.
keyPoints.quote: Modular monolith first, because billing workflows need consistency and are easier to learn in-process.
